stops.name: Hebron, the Cave of Machpelah
stops.campa: Three days after Jerusalem, on the ninth of Marcheshvan, Moses travels south to Hebron and comes, so far as the Crusader custodians of the shrine allow, before the Cave of Machpelah, where the tradition of three faiths at once places Abraham, Sarah, Isaac, Rebecca, Jacob, and Leah at rest. He prays among the patriarchs of his own line, in the presence, he believes, of the very bones from which his people descend. Like the sixth of Marcheshvan, the ninth becomes a fixed private holiday: two days a year, for the rest of his life, given wholly to thanksgiving for having stood on this ground at all.
stops.quote: On Sunday of the following week, the 9th of the month, I left Jerusalem and set out for Hevron, to visit the graves of our forefathers in the cave of the Machpelah.
stops.quote_source: Maimonides' colophon note on his journey to Hebron, 1165

stops.name: Alexandria, landfall in Egypt
stops.campa: The Holy Land under the Crusaders offers prayer but no living: little Jewish communal structure, no opening for a physician and scholar to support a family. Within months of Hebron, the family sails on to Egypt, landing first at Alexandria, the old Ptolemaic port whose library once held the learning Moses has spent his life absorbing at second hand through Arabic translation. Egypt lies under the Shi'ite Fatimid Caliphate, tolerant by comparison with the Almohads, and hosts an old, organized, prosperous Jewish community with a chief synagogue, a court, and a tradition of learning stretching back centuries. It will be the last stop of the exile.

stops.name: Fustat, the death of Maimon the father
stops.campa: The family moves on to Fustat, Old Cairo, where the community's institutions, a great synagogue, a rabbinic court, a network of merchants trading as far as India, offer the settled life Palestine could not. But the respite is brief: within the year of arrival Maimon ben Joseph, dayyan of Córdoba, refugee of two exiles, dies in the city that has finally received his family. Moses, not yet thirty, is now head of the household in fact as well as name, answerable for his sister, his younger brother David, and the fortunes of a family that has already lost everything once.

stops.name: Fustat, the Commentary on the Mishnah completed
stops.campa: After ten years of labor begun in his father's house in Córdoba and carried across every stage of the exile, Moses completes at thirty the Kitab al-Siraj, the Book of the Lamp, his Arabic commentary on the entire Mishnah, meant to open the oral law to readers who cannot follow the Talmud's tangled argument. Within its introduction to the tenth chapter of Sanhedrin he sets down, almost as an aside that will outlast the rest, thirteen principles he holds as the irreducible foundation of Jewish belief: one incorporeal God, true prophecy, an unchanging Torah, reward and punishment, the Messiah, and the resurrection of the dead.

stops.name: Fustat and Bilbays, the ransom of the captives
stops.campa: When the Crusader king Amalric storms Bilbays in the eastern Delta and carries off its Jews among the plunder, word reaches Fustat and Moses throws himself into pidyon shevuyim, the ransom of captives, which he will later rule in his own code outweighs even charity to the poor. He writes, solicits, and signs receipts in his own hand for funds raised community by community to buy back the enslaved. It is his first recorded public leadership in Egypt, years before any formal title, and it marks him, to a community that watched him arrive a penniless refugee, as a man to be trusted with its money and its people.
stops.quote: The redemption of captives receives priority over sustaining the poor and providing them with clothing. There is no mitzvah as great as the redemption of captives.
stops.quote_source: Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Matnot Aniyim 8:10 (his later codification of the principle he acted on at Bilbays)

stops.name: Fustat, appointed Nagid of Egyptian Jewry
stops.campa: The leadership shown over Bilbays, and the collapse of the Fatimid Caliphate that same year into the new Ayyubid order of Saladin, bring Moses formally to the headship of Egyptian Jewry: Nagid, invested with authority over the community's courts, its charities, its relations with the state. He is not yet forty. The office his family fled two countries to escape losing, held once by rabbis of Córdoba, is refounded in Cairo on a scale neither Córdoba nor Fez could have offered: chief of a community stretching from Alexandria to the Nile's first cataract.

stops.name: Fustat, the tidings of David's death
stops.campa: David, who has supported the family's scholarship by trading in gems so that Moses might study and write undistracted, sails from Egypt toward India some years earlier on a venture from which he does not return: a ship lost with all hands in the Indian Ocean, the family fortune and the fortunes of others gone down with it. When the news at last reaches Fustat, Moses collapses, bedridden for a year with fever and something close to madness. He will write, nearly a decade on, that he still cannot see his brother's handwriting or open one of his books without his heart failing within him.
stops.quote: The greatest misfortune that has befallen me during my entire life... was the demise of the saint, may his memory be blessed, who drowned in the Indian sea.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Yefet (Japheth) ben Eliyahu of Acre, c. 1185, recalling David's death

stops.name: Fustat, the labor on the Mishneh Torah begins
stops.campa: Even as he mourns and administers and practices medicine to keep the household solvent, Moses begins the work that will occupy the next decade: a complete code of Jewish law, written not in the language of learned debate but in clear Mishnaic Hebrew, so that any reader, without a library of Talmudic argument at hand, might know exactly what the law requires in every circumstance a Jewish life can meet. He calls it Mishneh Torah, Repetition of the Law, fourteen books for the whole of observance, arranged by subject rather than by the order the Talmud happens to take them up.

stops.name: Fustat, the Epistle to Yemen
stops.campa: Word comes from Jacob al-Fayyumi, leader of the Jews of Yemen, that a ruler there is forcing conversions and a false messiah has risen to exploit the community's terror. Moses answers with the Iggeret Teiman, a letter of history, consolation, and warning, tracing the long chain of persecution the Jewish people has survived from Egypt to the present hour and insisting that no forced apostasy and no premature messianic claim can break a covenant that has already outlasted every empire that tried it. Copied and recopied, it becomes scripture in miniature for communities under pressure across the Islamic world.
stops.quote: Much have they afflicted me from my youth up; but they have not prevailed against me.
stops.quote_source: Psalm 129:2, cited by Maimonides in the Epistle to Yemen, c. 1172

stops.name: Fustat, the Mishneh Torah completed
stops.campa: After ten years of labor, snatched between medical rounds and communal judgments, the fourteen books stand complete: a code covering the whole of Jewish law from the blessing over bread to the sacrifices of a rebuilt Temple, from the laws of theft to the reign of the Messianic king, every ruling stated in Moses's own clear Hebrew without citation of the sources behind it, so a student might hold in a few volumes what once required a lifetime in the Talmud's argument to extract. He closes it, in the humility the tradition expects of its greatest scholars, with his own name spelled in acrostic in the final lines.

stops.name: Fustat, the code contested
stops.campa: The very completeness of the code offends where it might have pleased: rabbis in Baghdad and Provence, led by figures like Samuel ben Ali, object that a Jew might now consult Moses's rulings alone and never open the Talmud that stands behind them, that the code threatens to make the argument itself, the give and take by which the law lives, obsolete. Moses defends the work by letter without retracting a word of it, holding that clarity for the ordinary reader is no crime and that scholars will go on arguing regardless of what any code says. The dispute over his authority will outlive him by generations.

stops.name: Fustat, physician to al-Qadi al-Fadil
stops.campa: Medicine, which Moses studied alongside law and philosophy in Córdoba and Fez, becomes in Egypt his second profession and eventually his livelihood, freeing the office of Nagid from dependence on communal fees. He is taken into the household of al-Qadi al-Fadil, secretary and chief counselor of the rising Ayyubid state, effectively its administrator behind Saladin's own name. His friend and colleague Ibn Jumay, the sultan's own physician, vouches for him among the Muslim medical establishment of Cairo, where a Jewish doctor's reputation must rest on results the court itself can verify.
